title: the Alvar hymns
hook: a list of things a group of girls won't do for a month, and what they lean on when they finally reach Krishna's door

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, Tiruppan was carried into the temple and looked at the Lord from the feet up, one part at a time. Who did you look at slowly? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.
screen: `FROM THE FEET UP.` · `TODAY: THE RULES OF A VOW.`

segments.voice: No ghee. No milk. A bath before dawn. No kohl on the eyes, no flowers in the hair. That's part of a list, and the people keeping it are girls of Krishna's cowherd village, setting out on a vow for the month of Margazhi. The list is a hymn. Andal sang it, one of the Alvars, in her Tiruppavai, the song of the dawn vow. Year three walked with those girls as they woke each other in the dark and went knocking at Krishna's door. Today we read two other pages of the same song: the rules they keep on the way, and what they say about themselves when they arrive.
screen: `NO GHEE. NO MILK.` → `NO KOHL, NO FLOWERS.` → `ANDAL'S TIRUPPAVAI.`

segments.voice: Early in the hymn, the girls set out how they'll keep the vow. They'll bathe early, before dawn. They'll go without ghee and without milk. They won't line their eyes or put flowers in their hair. They won't do what shouldn't be done. And they won't go carrying harmful words about anyone. Then the list turns from giving up to giving: they'll give alms and gifts, as much as they're able. So the vow isn't only about going without. It trims the comforts, guards the tongue, and opens the hand. Now go to the end of the hymn, where they finally stand before Krishna. You might expect them to list their merits: all those cold baths, all that missed ghee. They don't mention any of it. We follow the cows into the woods and eat there, they say. We're a cowherd clan with no learning at all. Our one good fortune is that you were born among us. And then the line Sri Vaishnava teachers keep coming back to: the bond between you and us can't be undone here, even if someone tried. We're children who don't know any better, they add. If, out of love, we called you by small names, don't be angry. Notice the order. A month of discipline, and when they reach the door, they don't hold it up. What they lean on is the bond. The vow got them out of bed in the dark. It isn't what they hand over at the door. That's the voice of this verse: plain, a little sheepish, and completely sure of the relationship.
screen: `BATHE BEFORE DAWN. NO GHEE, NO MILK.` · `NO HARMFUL WORDS. GIVE WHAT YOU CAN.` · `WE'RE COWHERDS WITH NO LEARNING.` · `THE BOND CAN'T BE UNDONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: arrive with the bond. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you're close to, or God if you pray. Notice any urge to show up with a list: what you've done for them, how hard you've tried, what you've given up. Let the list go quiet, one item at a time. Then rest in the plain fact of the bond itself, with nothing to show, the way the girls stood at the door. If a small, fond name for them comes to mind, let it come. The bell holds the time.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Andal's dawn vow: comforts trimmed, the tongue guarded, the hand open, and at the door, only the bond. Today's word.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Today, keep one rule from the girls' list: carry no harmful word about anyone, from morning to night. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In the month of Margazhi, Sri Vaishnava temples and households recite Andal's Tiruppavai before dawn, and teachers explain its verses on the rules of the vow and on the bond with the Lord that can't be undone.

our learning and our good deeds.

original.note: Tamil: the name of Andal's hymn of the dawn vow. Tamil, not Sanskrit, is the language of the Alvar hymns.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vow is a list of things you give up.
what it means: Andal's vow trims comforts, guards the tongue and opens the hand, and at the door the girls lean only on the bond.

what a scholar hears: the rules of the pavai vow early in the Tiruppavai, and the closing verse beginning karavaigal pin senru, with its bond, uravu, that 'can't be removed here', on which Sri Vaishnava commentators dwell.

notes: Editor: re-angled the whole lesson. The writer's version (waking verses, the drum, 'we came to belong to you') closely repeated year three's day 908, including its opening line; this version takes verse 2 (the rules of the vow) and verse 28 (no learning; the bond that can't be undone; small names) instead, and points back to day 908. The review now picks up day 1221 (Tiruppan). Games, sources, hook, practice and carry rewritten to match.

Verse 2's list (early bath; no ghee, no milk; no kohl, no flowers in the hair; not doing what shouldn't be done; not carrying harmful tales; alms and gifts as far as able) is paraphrased; a Tamil reader should confirm each item.

Verse 28 (karavaigal pin senru...) is paraphrased: following the cows to the forest to eat; a cowherd clan with no knowledge; the merit of Krishna born among them; the bond (uravu) can't be removed here; children who don't know, calling him by small names out of love; don't be angry. Confirm.
'The line Sri Vaishnava teachers keep coming back to' is framed loosely; a Keeper may tighten or cut it.
Andal's garland story was told in year one (day 269) and year three (day 907); the waking verses and drum turn in day 908; all avoided here.
Tamil spelling திருப்பாவை and the stress marking in 'say' should be checked by a Tamil reader.
